• Scientific name: Trichomycterus itatiayae Miranda Ribeiro, 1906
  • Synonym: Trichomycterus brasiliensis itatiayae
  • IUCN Red List: Least Concern (last assessed 2018)

South America: rivers in the Itatiaia mountains, upper reaches of the Paraíba do Sul River basin in Brazil, Rio de Janeiro State.

Type locality: Ribeirão da Tapera, Mont-Serrat, Itatiaia, about 22°27'S, 44°50'W, Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, elevation about 800 meters.
South America: Rivers in the Itatiaia Mountains, upper reaches of the Paraíba do Sul River basin, Brazil. Type locality: do Itatiaya, ...em afluente do Parahyba, Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil.

Trichomycterus itatiayae is endemic to coastal drainages in southwest Rio de Janeiro and southeast São Paulo, Paraíba do Sul River. The species is relatively abundant, but with restricted distribution. It occurs in areas of preservation and sustainable use.
This genus takes live or frozen food, and commercial dry prepared foods are also well accepted. Be careful not to overfeed. In nature, they feed on small invertebrates living at the bottom.
Unreported in the aquarium. There is no breeding report.
Etymology: Trichomycterus comes from the Greek trichos, meaning hair, and mykter, meaning nose, in reference to the barbels.

Etymology: The specific name itatiayae refers to the Itatiaia mountains, Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, the type locality.

IUCN Red List: As no significant threats to its population have been detected, the species has been categorised as Least Concern (LC) (IUCN 2022).

Trichomycteridae is a monophyletic group composed of eight subfamilies, 41 genera and approximately 207 species (Ferraris 2007). Seven subfamilies are demonstrably monophyletic groups, but Trichomycterinae is the largest and clearly a polyphyletic group (Wosiacki 2002). The genus Trichomycterus, said not to be monophyletic (de Pinna 1989), is the richest and most widely distributed of the family, with 113 valid species throughout South and Central America, on both sides of the Andes (de Pinna and Wosiacki 2003, Ferraris 2007). A considerable diversity of Trichomycterus occurs in the hydrographic basins of south and southeast Brazil, where 34 species have been described (Bockman et al. 2004).
